core_summary: This fundamental optics chapter details the physical laws governing light reflection and refraction. It analyzes image formation by spherical concave and convex mirrors using ray construction techniques, applying the New Cartesian Sign Convention, mirror formula, and magnification equation. It then investigates light refraction through glass slabs, Snell's law, refractive index, image formation by convex and concave lenses, the lens formula, and optical power of lenses measured in dioptres.
key_concepts: Laws of Reflection: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; incident ray, normal, and reflected ray lie in the same plane
Spherical mirror geometry: Pole (P), Center of Curvature (C), Radius of Curvature (R = 2f), Principal Focus (F), and Focal Length (f)
Image formation by Concave Mirrors (real/inverted except when object is between P & F) and Convex Mirrors (always virtual, erect, diminished)
Practical applications: Concave mirrors in searchlights, solar furnaces, shaving mirrors; Convex mirrors as rear-view vehicle mirrors
New Cartesian Sign Convention for distance measurements from optical pole/center along principal axis
Refraction of Light: Bending of light rays passing obliquely between optically transparent media of differing optical density
Snell's Law of Refraction: sin(i) / sin(r) = constant (refractive index n21 = v1 / v2)
Refraction through rectangular glass slab causing lateral displacement of emergent ray parallel to incident path
Spherical Lenses: Convex (converging) and Concave (diverging) lenses; ray diagram constructions for object placements
Lens Formula: (1/v) - (1/u) = (1/f) and Lens Magnification: m = (h'/h) = v/u
Power of a Lens: P = 1 / f(in meters), measured in Dioptres (D); positive for convex lenses and negative for concave lenses

key_terms.definition: The bouncing back of light rays when they strike a polished interface boundary.
The point on the principal axis where light rays parallel to the axis converge (concave mirror/convex lens) or appear to diverge from (convex mirror/concave lens).
The change in direction and speed of a light ray when passing obliquely from one transparent medium into another of different optical density.
The dimensionless ratio of light speed in vacuum (or air) to light speed in the specific material medium.
The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (c) to the speed of light in a given medium (v), n = c/v.
Mathematical relation between object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) for spherical mirrors: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
Mathematical relation between object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) for spherical lenses: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
The ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object produced by a mirror or lens.
The measure of convergence or divergence a lens imparts on light rays, defined as the reciprocal of focal length in meters (P = 1/f).
The SI unit of optical power of a lens having a focal length of 1 meter (1 D = 1 m^-1).

key_takeaways: Concave mirrors form real, inverted images for most positions, but yield an enlarged virtual erect image when object is placed within the focal length.
Convex mirrors provide a wide field of view by forming diminished, erect, virtual images behind the mirror.
Light bends towards the normal when entering an optically denser medium (slower speed) and away from the normal when entering a rarer medium (faster speed).
A negative magnification value indicates a real and inverted image, whereas a positive magnification indicates a virtual and erect image.
Net optical power of thin lenses in contact equals the algebraic sum of individual powers: P = P1 + P2 + P3.
